stories.headline: Denver Public Schools board member D.J. Torres resigns amid board infighting
stories.summary:
Denver Public Schools board member Donald "D.J." Torres resigned unexpectedly Thursday, less than 10 months after being elected to a seat that was not set to expire until 2029. Torres cited the persistent interpersonal conflict among board directors as his reason for stepping down, writing in a four-page resignation letter that he had "been pulled away too many times from focusing on kids."

The board accepted Torres' resignation during a virtual meeting Thursday and again delayed a vote on whether to censure fellow board member Monica Hunter until Oct. 8, pending the completion of an outside investigation into allegations that Hunter made antisemitic comments about a Jewish colleague. Board President Xóchitl Gaytán had levied numerous allegations of policy violations against both Torres and Hunter, including that Torres repeatedly missed board meetings.

The six remaining directors now have 60 days to appoint a replacement for Torres' seat. Rob Gould, president of the Denver Classroom Teachers Association, called the resignation "a wake-up call" to school board leadership, saying too much energy had been consumed by interpersonal conflict while urgent challenges facing students went unaddressed.

The turmoil comes at a difficult time for Colorado's largest K-12 district, which has been struggling to maintain stable governance. The board is expected to take up the Hunter censure vote at its Oct. 8 meeting.

stories.headline: Former Colorado Supreme Court Justice Melissa Hart dies
stories.summary:
Melissa Hart, a former Colorado Supreme Court justice who retired in January citing health concerns related to two concussions sustained in 2025, has died, the Colorado Judicial Branch announced Thursday. The cause of her death was not released. Hart served as a justice from 2017 to 2025 after being appointed by then-Gov. John Hickenlooper.

The Colorado Judicial Branch remembered Hart as bringing "a scholar's rigor and a teacher's compassion to the bench." Gov. Jared Polis said she would be remembered as a "fierce fighter for the rule of law" and praised her leadership in family law and access-to-justice efforts.

Hart was a Denver native who graduated from East High School before earning her undergraduate degree from Harvard-Radcliffe College and her law degree from Harvard Law School. During her tenure on the court she also served as an adjunct professor at both the University of Colorado Law School and the University of Denver Sturm College of Law.

In her resignation letter, Hart had expressed particular concern about access to civil justice for low- and middle-income Coloradans and said she intended to continue working with the Colorado Access to Justice Commission after leaving the bench. Denver-based attorney and Colorado Bar Association President Qusair Mohamedbhai described her as a respected colleague who advocated for attorneys and mentored the next generation of lawyers.

stories.headline: Jeffco road rage shooting leaves man in his 70s injured; suspect at large
stories.summary:
The Jefferson County Sheriff's Office is searching for a suspect who opened fire on a vehicle during a road rage incident Tuesday night, injuring a man in his 70s. The shooting occurred just after 9 p.m. near the Interstate 70 on-ramp from Colfax Avenue, as the victim and his wife were driving home to Arvada from Golden.

According to investigators, the suspect, driving a red four-door sedan, pulled behind the victim's car following an altercation and fired multiple shots. Five bullets struck the vehicle, including one that hit the driver in the back. Despite the injury, the man drove himself to a local hospital; his wife, who was in the passenger seat, was not hurt.

The victim's injuries are not considered life-threatening. Authorities said they have limited information on the suspect vehicle and are working to locate and review surveillance footage from the area that may have captured the incident.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office at 303-980-7300.

stories.headline: Aurora Human Trafficking Unit arrests 28 suspects, recovers 29 victims in first year
stories.summary:
The Aurora Police Department's Human Trafficking Unit arrested 28 suspects and recovered 29 victims, including 15 minors, in its first year of operation, the department announced Thursday. The unit was created in September 2025 and has launched 53 investigations since its inception, making it one of a few agencies in Colorado with a dedicated human trafficking team.

Among those arrested is Marshae Wheelock, 24, of Aurora, who is tied to numerous human trafficking and sexual exploitation cases spanning several years and involving multiple child victims. Wheelock recently accepted a plea deal in the 18th Judicial District and faces eight to 16 years in prison at a Nov. 6 sentencing hearing.

Investigators also arrested Aja Abney, 20, of Centennial; Dasjuan Goode, 38, of Aurora; and Damara Hester, 32, of Denver, in connection with an undercover operation involving the sexual exploitation of a 16-year-old girl. Goode remains in custody on a $75,000 bond while Abney and Hester were released on bail.

Investigations Bureau Commander Marc Paolino credited the small unit as a "force multiplier" in reducing victimization. Anyone with information about suspects or additional victims is encouraged to contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at (720) 913-7867.

stories.headline: Denver's Sam Gary Branch Library closed after hazmat team finds narcotics-related substance
stories.summary:
The Sam Gary Branch Library in Denver is temporarily closed following a hazmat investigation that led officials to discover a powerful narcotics-related substance inside the building. Denver Fire Department hazmat teams responded and set up a decontamination site while conducting testing and evaluation of the facility.

Further testing inside the library determined there was no longer any risk to the public, according to city officials. The library will remain closed until cleaning operations are complete.

The incident underscores ongoing concerns about drug-related issues affecting public facilities across the Denver metro area. Officials did not immediately release details about the specific substance found or how it was discovered.

stories.headline: Denver Post editorial urges 'no' vote on Amendment 81, which would require police to investigate immigration status of criminal suspects
stories.summary:
The Denver Post editorial board has come out against Amendment 81, a Colorado ballot measure that would require local law enforcement officers to investigate the immigration status of every person charged with a violent crime or any crime if the suspect has a prior felony conviction. If an investigation determines someone is in the country illegally — or if the investigation is inconclusive — police would be required to notify the Department of Homeland Security.

The editorial board acknowledged it has long supported cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE when agents present lawful warrants or final removal orders, but argued Amendment 81 goes too far by requiring officers to devote time and resources to immigration investigations on behalf of federal agents. The board cited a string of incidents in which federal immigration agents in Colorado have wrongfully detained U.S. citizens, violated court orders and used unmarked vehicles.

Among the incidents cited are the 2025 detention of a Utah teenager held illegally at an Aurora facility for two weeks, the month-long detention of a Durango man and his two children who had a pending asylum case, and the wrongful detention of a Denver Public Schools teacher. A federal judge ruled in September that immigration agents in Colorado had violated his court orders in several cases.

Amendment 81 is the first measure Colorado voters will see on the November ballot. The editorial board's stance adds to an ongoing public debate over the balance between state and local authority and federal immigration enforcement in Colorado.

stories.headline: Former RK Industries Denver headquarters sells for $16.78 million, clearing way for 329-unit apartment development
stories.summary:
The former RK Industries headquarters at 3800 Xanthia St. in Denver has sold for $16.78 million to multifamily developer The Garrett Cos., which plans to build a 329-unit apartment community on the approximately 10-acre site. A warranty deed filed with the city Friday confirmed the transaction. Construction is expected to begin later this year, with completion targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027.

The property is located in the Central Park master-planned community. The Garrett Cos. also has plans for a second development phase on an additional five acres of the site. Eric Roth and Martin Roth of CBRE represented the seller.

RK Industries relocated its headquarters to a 154,488-square-foot facility in Aurora at 3301 Lewiston St., a move supported by $24.4 million in state tax incentives aimed at retaining the company's expansion in Colorado. The company projects creating more than 1,700 jobs over the next eight years.

The Garrett Cos. has several other Colorado projects underway, including apartment communities in Aurora, Broomfield and Parker, as well as a planned redevelopment of a vacant Centennial office property into 368 multifamily units.

stories.headline: Thompson Thrift to build 284-unit luxury apartment and retail complex in Golden
stories.summary:
National real estate developer Thompson Thrift has announced plans to develop Alasso, a mixed-use project featuring 284 luxury apartment homes and approximately 20,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space in Golden, roughly 15 miles west of Denver. The project will be situated on about 9.3 acres on S. Golden Road and is expected to welcome its first residents in early 2028.

Alasso will consist of two four-story residential buildings, a 430-space structured parking garage and ground-floor commercial space intended for restaurant, fitness, service and other neighborhood uses. Units will range from studios to three-bedroom apartments with up to 1,730 square feet of living space.

Thompson Thrift Managing Partner Josh Purvis cited Golden's strong employment base, connectivity and high demand for quality rental housing as key factors in selecting the site. Major nearby employers include the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Molson Coors, Colorado School of Mines and CoorsTek.

Golden is considered one of the most supply-constrained multifamily submarkets in Colorado, with restrictive zoning and limited available land. Average home values within three miles of the Alasso site exceed $850,000, creating what developers describe as a significant gap between the cost of renting and owning.

stories.headline: Nederland seeks $20 million in donations to salvage Eldora Mountain Resort purchase
stories.summary:
The town of Nederland announced it needs $20 million in philanthropic donations to complete its planned $120 million purchase of Eldora Mountain Resort, acknowledging that prospective bondholders have raised concerns about the deal's financial structure. In a letter posted to the town website Wednesday, Mayor Nichole Sterling and the board of trustees said the donations are necessary to reduce the overall debt load and provide stronger security tied to the asset.

The purchase agreement with Eldora's parent company, Powdr Corp., has expired, though the two parties are still in talks and an updated agreement could be reached. The deal, now expected to take the form of a sale-leaseback arrangement with Powdr continuing to support operations, was originally supposed to close by the end of April. Nederland has repeatedly declined to release the bond offering memorandum that would shed more light on the concerns raised by bondholders.

The town announced its letter of intent to buy the ski area in July 2025 and the board of trustees formally approved the $120 million purchase — roughly $80,000 per resident — in January. Higher-than-projected interest rates, now modeled at approximately 8.5 percent versus an initial estimate of 7.5 percent, have added to the financing challenges. Dismal snowfall last winter also contributed to a steep drop in skier visits, prompting bondholders to ask for more conservative financial modeling.

Philanthropic dollars would fund capital improvements including a new mountaintop lodge and summer operations, with naming rights for ski runs offered as an incentive to major donors. Nederland said separating those projects from bond-regulated payments would give the mountain more flexibility in poor snow years.

stories.headline: New program subsidizes first mile of Veo bike and scooter rides to two Denver transit stations
stories.summary:
A new pilot program launched Thursday that automatically subsidizes the first mile of Veo shared bike and scooter rides that end at two Denver transit stations, marking what organizers say is the first such program in the country. The two-year initiative is funded through an RTD grant supplemented by $65,000 in additional funding.

The program is designed to improve first-mile connectivity to public transit, encouraging riders to use shared micromobility options to reach transit hubs rather than driving. Veo scooters and bikes are available on streets throughout the city.

Transportation officials say the subsidy could help increase RTD ridership by making it easier and cheaper for commuters to complete the last leg of a trip to a train or bus station. The specific stations included in the pilot were not detailed in initial reports.

stories.headline: Most Western Slope fire restrictions lifted as cooler temperatures, rain arrive
stories.summary:
Most Western Slope counties have lifted fire restrictions following cooler temperatures and increased rainfall across the region, according to CPR News. The easing of restrictions comes after a severe drought earlier in the season contributed to wildfires across Colorado and forced many jurisdictions to implement Stage 1 or higher restrictions.

Routt County, Steamboat Springs and El Paso County have rescinded Stage 1 fire restrictions following recent precipitation, while Grand County is maintaining its Stage 1 restrictions. State health officials have authorized open vegetative burning during designated afternoon hours for permit holders in areas without local bans.

No red flag warnings or fire weather watches are currently in effect across Colorado, and overall fire potential is rated low to lowest statewide. Dry conditions are expected to persist under regional high pressure, with gusty southerly winds on the eastern plains and some elevated fire danger near the Wyoming border.

stories.headline: Rockies rank offseason needs after fourth straight 100-loss season
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies concluded the 2026 season with a 58-104 record, their fourth consecutive campaign with at least 100 losses, and are now turning to a demanding offseason to address multiple roster deficiencies. Starting pitching has been identified as the most pressing need, consistent with prior seasons of struggle on the mound.

The team's financial commitments heading into next year are relatively light, with Kris Bryant the only player currently slated to earn more than $8.5 million. Only four players have guaranteed major-league contracts beyond their arbitration years, giving the organization flexibility but also underscoring the depth of the rebuild.

Positives from the season include continued development from younger players, including catcher Hunter Goodman, who homered in late-September action. The organization has framed its approach as focusing on one position at a time as it works through a prolonged rebuilding process.

The Rockies have not made the postseason since 2018, and the franchise faces mounting pressure from fans and analysts to accelerate the timeline for competitiveness at Coors Field.

topStory.headline: France School Protests Spread Nationwide; 400 Schools Closed, Nearly 3,000 Detained
topStory.summary:
A wave of student protests has forced the closure of approximately 400 of France's 3,700 secondary schools as of Friday, with the Ministry of National Education reporting that 564 schools and educational establishments have been disrupted or subject to industrial action since the start of the day. Authorities reported 1,949 arrests on Thursday alone, bringing the total number of detentions since the unrest began to nearly 3,000, the vast majority of them minors between the ages of 15 and 18. Many schools have pivoted to remote learning in response to the closures ordered by local police prefects.

The protests, which originated last week in the Paris region, have spread to major cities including Lille, Lyon, Nantes, Marseille, and Strasbourg. French Education Minister Édouard Geffray confirmed that 40 headteachers were among 65 public school staff members injured, with principals targeted, assaulted, or harassed while attempting to maintain order at school gates. A total of 305 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters were also injured during heavy clashes on Thursday, and at least 170 students have been hurt since demonstrations began. In Marseille, a crowd surrounded a fire engine and set it ablaze after forcing the crew to flee.

More than 100 secondary schools have sustained significant structural damage, with protesters lighting fires outside building entrances in Nantes and Rouen and barricading entryways with trash bins and bicycles. Approximately 30 university campuses were also blockaded by older students joining the movement. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has convened emergency crisis meetings to address the escalating situation.

Students and the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the main student union driving the demonstrations, say the protests are a response to systemic failures in the French public education system, including severe teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms frequently exceeding 34 students, and deteriorating school infrastructure. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin has directed local prosecutors to pursue civil liability claims against parents of minors responsible for property damage. With protests continuing into the weekend and hundreds more schools potentially affected, French authorities face mounting pressure to address the underlying grievances while restoring order.
